1:1: When Peter calls his readers exiles, he could mean: (1) they are exiles because they are far away from their true home in heaven; (2) they are exiles because they were forced to leave their homes and go far away to Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia.

Here, dispersion could refer to: (1) groups of Gentile Christians who were spread throughout the world instead of in their true home in heaven. In this case, dispersion would have a similar meaning to exiles and would add emphasis; (2) the groups of Jewish people who were spread across the Greek-speaking world that was outside of the land of Israel, which is the common technical meaning for this word.
Πόντου, Γαλατίας, Καππαδοκίας, Ἀσίας, καὶ Βιθυνίας
Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia are names of Roman provinces that were located in what is now the country of Turkey.
1:2: This phrase could mean: (1) God had determined what would happen ahead of time; (2) God knew what would happen ahead of time.
εἰς ὑπακοὴν καὶ ῥαντισμὸν αἵματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
Here, obedience could refer to: (1) obeying God; (2) obeying Jesus Christ.

Peter uses sprinkling to refer to believers being in a covenant relationship with God. Just as Moses sprinkled blood on the people of Israel in Exodus 24:1–11 to symbolize that they were joining in a covenant relationship with God, believers are joined in a covenant relationship with God by means of Jesus’ death. Moses also sprinkled blood on the priests to set them apart to serve God as priests (Leviticus 8:30).
Here, blood refers to the death of Jesus.
In this culture, letter writers would offer a good wish for the recipient before introducing the main business of the letter.
Peter speaks of Grace and peace as if they were objects that could increase in size or number.
1:3: The phrase born again is a metaphor that refers to spiritual rebirth.
Peter uses living to describe hope that is certain and will not lead to disappointment.
1:4: κληρονομίαν ἄφθαρτον, καὶ ἀμίαντον, καὶ ἀμάραντον
Peter uses inheritance to refer to what we will receive in heaven. This could refer to: (1) The promise of God that we will live forever with him; (2) future blessings in heaven after this life.
1:5: Here, the last time refers to “the day of the Lord,” which is the time when Jesus returns to the world to judge everyone and vindicate those who believe in him.
1:7: Here Peter speaks of faith, as if it were gold that is refined by passing it through fire. He also uses fire to refer to the hardships that test how well believers trust in Christ.
In this clause Peter means that faith is more valuable than gold because faith lasts forever but gold does not, even if it is refined by someone passing it through fire.
Peter assumes that his readers will know that he is referring to the future revelation of Jesus Christ, when Jesus returns to earth.
1:8: Here, inexpressible and filled with glory mean basically the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize how great the joy is.
1:9: Here Peter speaks of salvation as if it were an object that someone could receive.
Here, souls refers to the individual Christians to whom Peter is writing this letter.
1:10: The phrases searched and inquired carefully mean basically the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize how hard the prophets tried to understand this salvation.
1:11: The word translated as whom could also be translated as “what.” In that case, “what” would refer to the time when salvation would take place and what time would then refer to the specific circumstances.
This could indicate: (1) the time when the Spirit of Christ was revealing information to the prophets; (2) the means by which the Spirit of Christ was revealing information to the prophets.
1:12: This phrase indicates the means by which the evangelists proclaimed the gospel to Peter’s readers. Peter uses the Holy Spirit here to refer specifically to the Holy Spirit’s work of giving those evangelists the ability or power to proclaim the gospel effectively.
Here, things refers to what God had revealed to the prophets and some evangelists had proclaimed to Peter’s readers.
Peter uses look to refer to getting a clearer understanding of what God has revealed about salvation. This does not mean that the angels do not understand salvation at all.
1:13: ἀναζωσάμενοι τὰς ὀσφύας τῆς διανοίας ὑμῶν
Girding up the loins is an idiom that means to prepare to work hard. It comes from the custom of tucking the bottom of one’s robe into a belt around the waist in order to move with ease.
Here Peter uses sober to refer to mental clarity and alertness.
Here Peter speaks of grace as if it were an object that could be brought to people.
Here, the grace refers to salvation, as it also does in 1:10.
1:14: Here Peter uses children to refer to people who love and obey God. The relationship between God and those who love him is like the relationship between a father and his children.
1:17: Here Peter speaks of his readers as if they were people living in a foreign land far away from their homes. Like people living away from home, so are Christians living away from their home in heaven.
1:18: ἐκ τῆς ματαίας ὑμῶν ἀναστροφῆς πατροπαραδότου
Here, handed down refers to one generation teaching futile behavior to another generation, as if that behavior were an object that could be passed by hand from one person to another.
1:19: Peter uses the precious blood of Christ to refer to Jesus’ death.

Peter compares Jesus’ blood to the blood of the lambs that the Jewish priests sacrificed to God because of the people’s sins. The point of this comparison is that Jesus died as a sacrifice so that God would forgive people’s sins.
The words unblemished and spotless mean basically the same thing. Peter uses this repetition to emphasize that Christ was completely perfect and sinless.
1:20: This phrase could mean: (1) God had determined what Christ would do; (2) God knew what Christ would do ahead of time.
Here, having been revealed refers to the first time Jesus came to the earth.
Here, the last of the times refers to the final period of history which began when Jesus came to the earth for the first time. This period will end when Jesus returns to earth.
1:21: Here, to raise him is an idiom for causing someone who has died to become alive again.
1:22: Having purified refers to being forgiven for sins. In the Bible, sin is often referred to as something that makes people dirty, and the forgiveness for sin is referred to as the removal of that dirt. God is the one who forgives sins and purifies those who believe in Jesus. However, here Peter is referring to his readers’ responsibility in their salvation, which is the responsibility to repent and believe that the gospel is true.
Here, the truth refers to the true teaching about Jesus, which includes the command to repent and believe the gospel.
ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας, ἀλλήλους ἀγαπήσατε ἐκτενῶς

Peter uses heart here to refer to a person’s thoughts or emotions. The word from indicates that the heart must be the source of the love that Peter is telling his readers to have. Therefore, this phrase has a similar meaning to the word “sincere” in the previous clause.
1:23: The word seed usually refers to either the seed of a plant or the sperm cell of a man, which is used to produce a baby. However, here Peter uses seed as a metaphor. It could refer to: (1) the word of God mentioned later in the verse. In this case, Peter is saying what the word of God is not; (2) physical human birth, in which case the meaning is similar to the idea expressed in John 1:13.
Here Peter uses word to describe the gospel message that came from God and was proclaimed to Peter’s readers by using words.
Here, living and enduring mean basically the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize that God’s word is permanent.
1:24: Here Peter quotes Isaiah using the term flesh to refer to human beings in general, which are made of flesh.
Peter quotes Isaiah using glory to refer to whatever is beautiful or magnificent about humankind.
In this clause the prophet Isaiah continues the comparison between humankind and grass. Just like grass dies quickly, so human beings only live a short time.
In this clause the prophet Isaiah continues the comparison between the glory of humankind and flowers. Just like a flower dies and falls to the ground, so does the beauty of mankind disappear.
1:25: Peter quotes Isaiah using word to describe all that God has spoken by using words. This general reference to God’s word would include what God had said about the Messiah.
Here Peter uses word in the same specific sense as in 1:23. It is not the general meaning of word used earlier in the verse.
2:1: Peter speaks of these sinful actions as if they were objects that people could put aside the way people remove dirty clothing.
2:2: ὡς ἀρτιγέννητα βρέφη τὸ λογικὸν ἄδολον γάλα ἐπιποθήσατε
The point of this comparison is that Peter wanted his readers to desire knowledge of God’s word just as newborn babies desire milk.

The word translated as rational could also be translated as “pertaining to the word”; it refers to the word of God. Peter speaks of the word of God as if it were rational milk that nourishes children.
Peter speaks of believers advancing in the knowledge of God and faithfulness to him as if they were children growing up.
Here, salvation refers to when Jesus returns and God completes the salvation of his people. Peter also uses this meaning for salvation in 1:5.
2:3: Peter uses tasted to refer to personally experiencing something.
2:4: (2) a command, in which case “being built up” in the next verse would also be a command.
Peter refers to Jesus as if he were a stone in a building.

Peters speaks of a stone as if it were living. This could refer to: (1) a stone that is alive. This interpretation emphasizes the fact that Jesus is alive even though he had died; (2) a stone that gives life. This interpretation emphasizes the fact that Jesus gives eternal life to everyone who believes in him.
2:5: αὐτοὶ ὡς λίθοι ζῶντες οἰκοδομεῖσθε, οἶκος πνευματικὸς

Peter uses stones to refer to his readers, people who believe in Jesus. Just as people in the Old Testament used stones to build the temple that God dwelled in, God is using believers to bring together a group of people in whom he will dwell.

Peters uses stones as if they were living. This emphasizes the fact that Peter’s readers have eternal life because they believe in Jesus. In this verse, living cannot mean to give life, because only God can give life.
(2) a command, in which case “coming to him” in the previous verse would also be a command.
εἰς ἱεράτευμα ἅγιον ἀνενέγκαι πνευματικὰς θυσίας

Here Peter speaks of believers as if they were part of a priesthood and as if their good deeds and acts of worship were sacrifices offered to God. Just as the priests in the Old Testament offered sacrifices to God, so should believers do good deeds and worship God.
This could mean: (1) the sacrifices are of a spiritual, rather than physical, nature; (2) the sacrifices are offered by the power of the Holy Spirit.
2:6: Here the quotation of scripture that occurs next in the verse is spoken of as if it were a person who stands.
Peter quotes Isaiah using Behold to call his readers to pay attention to what he is about to say.
Here God refers to the Messiah as if he were not only a stone, but even the most important stone in a building, the cornerstone.
2:7: The phrase translated as the honor could also be translated as “precious,” in which case it would refer to the “cornerstone” in the previous verse.
The author uses stone to refer to the Messiah, and he uses builders to refer to those who rejected Jesus.
This phrase has the same meaning as “cornerstone” in the previous verse. It refers to the most important stone in a building. Here it refers specifically to the Messiah.
2:8: Peter quotes Isaiah speaking of the Messiah as if he were a stone or rock that people tripped over. Peter means that many people would be offended by Jesus’ teachings and reject him.
These two phrases mean almost the same thing. Isaiah says the same thing twice, in slightly different ways, to emphasize that people will be offended by this stone.
Here, the word refers to the gospel message, which includes the command to repent and believe the gospel.
Here, stumble could refer to: (1) being offended by the gospel, which is the meaning in the rest of this verse; (2) being judged for rejecting the gospel.
Here, disobeying refers to disobeying the command to repent and believe the gospel, which is part of the gospel message. Therefore, this disobeying means refusing to believe the gospel.
Here, which refers back to the previous part of this sentence. Those who do not believe in Jesus were appointed to stumble and disobey the word.
2:9: This could refer to: (1) members of a priesthood who are also members of the king’s family; (2) a priesthood which serves the king.
ἐκ σκότους … εἰς τὸ θαυμαστὸν αὐτοῦ φῶς
Here, darkness refers to the condition of people who do not know God and are sinful, and light refers to the condition of people who know God and are righteous.
2:11: General Information: Peter begins to tell his readers how to live Christian lives.
Here, foreigners and exiles mean basically the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize that Christians on this earth are far away from their home in heaven.
Peter uses foreigners here to refer to his Christian readers. Just like a foreigner is not in his homeland, so are Christians not at home while living on the earth.
Here, fleshly refers to a person’s sinful nature.
Peter speaks of fleshly desires as if they were soldiers trying to destroy the spiritual life of believers.
2:12: Peter uses Gentiles here to refer to people who are not Christians. Just like a Gentile was not a member of the Jewish people, so people who are not Christians are not members of God’s people.
This phrase is an idiom that refers to the time when God will judge all people.
2:13: Here, the Lord refers to Jesus. This phrase could mean: (1) we should do this to follow the example of Jesus, who also obeyed human authorities; (2) we should do this to honor Jesus.
2:16: Here, covering could refer to: (1) something to prevent people from knowing about one’s evil deeds; (2) an excuse or pretext to do evil deeds.
2:17: Here, brotherhood refers to all Christian believers.
2:18: General Information: Peter begins to speak specifically to people who were slaves who worked in people’s houses.
The words good and gentle mean similar things. Peter uses this repetition to emphasize that such masters treat their servants very kindly.
Here, crooked ones is used to refer to people who act dishonestly or unjustly as if their morals were an object that could be bent or twisted.
2:19: Peter assumes that his readers will know that he is referring to finding favor with God, which is what he states in the next verse.
Here, God refers to who God is and what he requires from his people.
2:20: ποῖον γὰρ κλέος, εἰ ἁμαρτάνοντες καὶ κολαφιζόμενοι ὑπομενεῖτε
Peter is not asking for information, but is using the question form here to emphasize that there is nothing praiseworthy about suffering for doing something wrong.
2:21: Here, this refers back to what Peter stated at the end of the previous verse. Believers are called by God to endure suffering while doing what is good.
Peter uses follow in his footsteps to refer to following Jesus’ example about enduring suffering.
2:22: οὐδὲ εὑρέθη δόλος ἐν τῷ στόματι αὐτοῦ
Peter quotes Isaiah referring to deceit as if it were an object that could be found inside someone’s mouth.
οὐδὲ εὑρέθη δόλος ἐν τῷ στόματι αὐτοῦ
Peter quotes Isaiah describing something the Messiah would say by association with his mouth, which he would use to say something. In this case it is something the Messiah did not say.
2:23: Here, the one judging justly refers to God. This means that Jesus trusted God to punish those who reviled him or to prove that he was innocent.
2:24: ὃς τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν αὐτὸς ἀνήνεγκεν
Peter uses the word himself here to emphasize that Jesus alone is the one who bore our sins.
Peter uses bore our sins to refer to Jesus being punished for our sins as if sins were an object that he carried on his body.
Peter uses tree to refer to the cross on which Jesus died, which was made of wood.

Here, having died to sins is a metaphor that means to no longer be controlled by sin. Like a dead person is free from sinning because they are no longer alive, so believers are free to stop sinning because Jesus bore the punishment for their sins.
Here, wounds refers to all the suffering Jesus endured when he was beaten and killed on the cross.
Here, healed could mean: (1) being freed from the penalty and power of sin, which could include physical healing; (2) being forgiven for their sins and having a restored relationship with God.
2:25: Peter speaks about his readers before they believed in Christ as if they had been similar to lost sheep that were wandering around aimlessly.
τὸν ποιμένα καὶ ἐπίσκοπον τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν
Peter uses shepherd and overseer to refer to Jesus. Just as a shepherd protects his sheep and an overseer takes care of his workers, Jesus protects and takes care of those who trust in him.
3:1: General Information: In 3:1–6 Peter gives instructions specifically to women who are wives.
Here, being disobedient to the word could refer to: (1) refusing to believe the gospel message, as in 2:8; (2) disobeying the commands God gave in his word.
Here, won is an idiom that means that the unbelieving husbands will become believers in Jesus.
Here, word refers to anything the wives might say to their husbands about the gospel message.
3:2: This could refer to: (1) the wives’ sincere and honest behavior; (2) the wives’ sexually chaste behavior.
3:4: Here, hidden man and heart both refer to a person’s thoughts or emotions.
Here, quiet means “peaceful” or “calm.” It does not mean the opposite of loud.
Here, spirit refers to a person’s attitude or temperament.
ὅ ἐστιν ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ πολυτελές
Peter refers to God’s opinion as if it were a person standing directly in front of him.
3:5: Peter speaks of the attitude of the holy women as if it were something with which they adorned themselves.
3:6: Peter uses a Hebrew idiom here in which people are said to be the children of someone who has qualities similar to theirs. Women who believe and who act like Sarah acted are thought of as if they were her actual children.
3:7: General Information: In this verse Peter gives instructions specifically to men who are husbands.

Here Peter refers to women as if they were weaker containers. The word container is a term used to refer to both men and women in the Bible (Acts 9:15). Just as clay pots can break easily, so are human beings weak. Here Peter specifically refers to women as weaker containers because woman are usually physically weaker than men.
Peter speaks of the grace of life as if it were something that people inherit.
3:8: General Information: In 3:8–12 Peter writes instructions to all believers.
3:9: Peter uses paying back to refer to responding to the actions of another person as if one was returning money to that person for those actions.
Here, this could refer to: (1) blessing earlier in the verse; (2) inherit a blessing later in the verse “to this you were called so that”
Peter speaks of experiencing God’s blessing as if one is receiving an inheritance.
3:10: These two phrases mean basically the same thing and emphasize the desire to have a good life.
Peter quotes David speaking of experiencing a good lifetime as to see good days.
Peter quotes David using the words tongue and lips to refer to the person who is speaking.
3:11: Here, turn away from is a metaphor that means to avoid doing something.
The phrases seek peace and pursue it mean basically the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize the importance of living peacefully with other people.
Here, peace refers to peaceful relationships between people.
3:12: Here, eyes being on someone is an idiom that refers to God acting favorably toward someone by taking care of that person.
Here, ears being toward someone’s request is an idiom that refers to God listening to that person’s request.
The idea that the Lord listens to the requests of righteous people also implies that he responds to those requests.
Here, the face being against someone is an idiom that refers to one person opposing another person.
3:13: Connecting Statement: In 3:13–22 Peter teaches the believers how to behave when unbelievers persecute them.
Peter is not asking for information, but is using the question form here to emphasize that it is unlikely that someone would harm them if they did good things.
3:14: τὸν δὲ φόβον αὐτῶν, μὴ φοβηθῆτε μηδὲ ταραχθῆτε
These two phrases mean the same thing. Peter states the same idea twice in order to emphasize that believers should not be afraid of people who persecute them.
3:15: Peter uses sanctify the Lord Christ to refer to acknowledging Christ’s holiness.
Here, hearts refers to the thoughts or emotions of Peter’s readers.
Peter uses word to refer to an answer or explanation spoken by using words.
Peter speaks of hope as if it were something that could be inside a person.
3:16: ὑμῶν τὴν ἀγαθὴν ἐν Χριστῷ ἀναστροφήν
Here, in Christ refers to being a Christian.
3:17: εἰ θέλοι τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ
Peter uses the will of God to refer to God himself.
3:18: Here, sins implies the sins of people other than Jesus, because Jesus never sinned.
Here, flesh refers to Christ’s body, which was made of flesh. Peter is saying that the body of Christ was killed.

Here, spirit could refer to: (1) the Holy Spirit, in which case this phrase would indicate the means by which Jesus was made alive; (2) Jesus’ spiritual existence, in which case this phrase would be referring to the spiritual realm that is in contrast to the physical realm referred to with the phrase “in the flesh.”
3:19: Here, which refers to “spirit” in the previous verse. As in the previous verse, this could refer to: (1) the Holy Spirit; (2) Jesus’ spiritual existence.

(2) the spirits of people who died during the flood that occurred in Noah’s time. This interpretation is a less likely to be correct because Peter never refers to people as spirits, but rather “souls,” as in the next verse.

Here Peter uses prison as a metaphor. It could refer to: (1) a place where God imprisoned certain evil spirits whom he will judge when he judges the whole world (See: 2 Peter 2:4–5; Jude 6–7); (2) the place where sinful people go when they die.
3:20: Peter uses patience of God to refer to God himself.
Here Peter uses days of Noah to refer to the time period when Noah was alive.
3:21: ὃ καὶ ὑμᾶς ἀντίτυπον νῦν σῴζει βάπτισμα
Here, antitype refers to one thing that is an analogy for another thing. In this context the “water” from the previous verse is an analogy for baptism.

Here Peter uses baptism to refer to the faith in Jesus that believers profess when they are baptized. The Bible clearly states that God saves people by grace through faith, not by any work like baptism (Ephesians 2:8–9). See the discussion in the introduction for this chapter.
Here, Peter uses flesh to refer to a person’s physical body that is made of flesh.
Here the phrase a good conscience means Peter’s readers do not feel guilty because they know that God has forgiven their sins.
3:22: Here, Peter uses right hand to refer to the place located at the right side of God in heaven.
In this culture, the place at the right side of a ruler was a position of honor.
ὑποταγέντων αὐτῷ ἀγγέλων, καὶ ἐξουσιῶν, καὶ δυνάμεων
The words angels, authorities, and powers are all terms for the ranks of supernatural beings, both angelic and demonic.
4:1: Here, flesh refers to the human body, which is made of flesh.
Here Peter uses arm yourselves to refer to preparing one’s mind for something. As soldiers get their weapons ready for battle, so should Christians be mentally prepared to suffer for their faith.
Here Peter uses the same way of thinking to refer to Jesus’ way of thinking when he suffered.

Here, ceased from sin means “no longer living with a sinful mindset.” The idea is that suffering because of one’s faith indicates that a person is not living sinfully. Christians are often persecuted by unbelievers because they refuse to act sinfully. This phrase does not mean that Christians who suffer never sin.
4:2: Peter uses time in the flesh to refer to a person’s lifetime.
4:3: Here Peter uses Gentiles to refer to sinful people who do not know God. See the discussion of this term in the introduction for this chapter.
Peter speaks of these different sins as if they were places that his readers had formerly lived in.
4:4: Peter uses running into to refer to being eager to participate in sinful acts with unbelievers.
Peter uses outpouring to refer to acting sinfully to such a high degree that it is as if sin were pouring out of the person like a flood.
The word recklessness refers to dangerous behavior that shows that a person does not care about the consequences of his actions.
4:5: Here Peter uses give to refer to speaking something.
Here Peter uses word to refer to an explanation that they would speak using words.
Here, the one being ready to judge could refer to: (1) God; (2) Christ.
The phrase living and dead ones refers to all people, whether they are still alive or have died.
4:6: Here, dead ones refers to people who heard the gospel while they were alive but had died by the time Peter wrote this letter. Some people believe that this clause means that Jesus went to hell and preached the gospel to people who had died before Jesus himself died on the cross. However, that idea would contradict the statement in Hebrews 9:27 that “men are appointed to die once, and after that, the judgment.” The Bible does not state that God gave anyone a second chance to believe in Jesus after they had already died.
Here Peter uses in the flesh to refer to a person’s lifetime.
Here, live refers to experiencing eternal life.
4:7: Here, the end of all things refers to the end of the world, when Jesus returns and judges everyone.
Peter uses has come near to refer to something that will happen soon.
The words translated as sound mind and sober mean basically the same thing. Peter uses them to emphasize the need to think clearly since the end of the world is near.
4:8: Peter describes love as if it were a person who could cover something up, and he describes sins as if they were objects that could be covered up. This clause, covers up, means that people who love others will forgive them for the sins that they commit against them.
4:9: The word hospitable refers to showing kindness to and providing for the needs of guests and travelers. This was especially important in Peter’s time because inns were dangerous places where people did many immoral activities, so Christians could not stay in them.
Here Peter uses a figure of speech that expresses a strong positive meaning by using a negative word together with a word that is the opposite of the intended meaning.
4:10: Here, gift refers to special spiritual abilities that God gives to believers.
ὡς καλοὶ οἰκονόμοι ποικίλης χάριτος Θεοῦ
Peter uses stewards to refer to Christians using spiritual abilities from God to serve other believers as if they were managing resources for a boss.
4:12: Peter refers to suffering Christians as if they were gold being refined by being passed through a fire. In the same way that fire refines gold, trials test and strengthen a Christian’s faith.
4:13: ἐν τῇ ἀποκαλύψει τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ
Here, the revelation of his glory refers to the time in the future when Jesus returns to earth and judges everyone.
The words rejoice and glad mean basically the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize the intensity of joy.
4:14: τὸ τῆς δόξης καὶ τὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ Πνεῦμα
Here, of glory and of God both refer to the Holy Spirit.

Here, rests on you is an idiom that refers to the Holy Spirit continually dwelling within Christians. Peter borrowed this language from Isaiah 11:2 where it originally referred to the Holy Spirit dwelling in the Messiah. The Holy Spirit dwells in the Messiah as well as in those who believe in the Messiah (John 1:33; 14:16–17). The Holy Spirit who dwells within believers provides strength and comfort when believers are persecuted for their faith.
4:15: Here, meddler refers to a person who gets involved with the affairs of others without having a right to do so.
4:16: Here, this name refers to the title “Christian” mentioned earlier in the verse.
4:17: Here Peter uses household to refer to all believers as if they were a family that belongs to God.
Peter is not asking for information, but is using the question form here to emphasize that God’s judgment will be more severe for people who reject the gospel than for those who believe it.
Here, end refers to the final result of the lives of people who do not believe in Jesus.
Here, disobeying refers to disobeying the command to repent and believe the gospel, which is part of the gospel message.
4:18: ὁ ἀσεβὴς καὶ ἁμαρτωλὸς ποῦ φανεῖται
Peter is not asking for information, but is using the question form here to emphasize that ungodly people will suffer much more than believers do.
The words ungodly and sinner mean basically the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize the wickedness of these people.
5:1: General Information: In 5:1–4 Peter speaks directly to men who are leaders in the churches.
In 5:1–5 the words elder and elders refer specifically to church leaders, who were often older men. Here these words do not refer to old men in general.
The phrase the glory being about to be revealed refers to Christ’s glorious return to earth in the future.
5:2: Here Peter uses Shepherd to refer to leading and taking care of believers, and he uses flock to refer to those believers. Elders who lead assemblies of believers should take care of those believers like shepherds take care of their sheep.
The phrases not under compulsion and willingly mean the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize that Peter wants church leaders to voluntarily take care of believers.
This phrase refers to acting according to God’s will or requirements.
The phrases not greedily and eagerly mean basically the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize that Peter wants church leaders to eagerly take care of believers.
5:3: Here Peter uses lording it over to refer to acting toward people in a harsh and controlling manner, as if someone were a harsh master who abuses his servants.
5:4: Here Peter speaks of Jesus as if he were a Shepherd who has authority over all the leaders of the assemblies of believers. Peter told those leaders to shepherd their flocks in 5:2.

Here, crown refers to a symbol of victory. It does not refer to the type of crown that kings wear. In ancient times an athlete would receive this crown as a reward for winning a competition. Those crowns were often made of leaves or flowers that would fade. Unlike those victory crowns, the reward that God gives will be unfading, which means that it will last forever.
5:5: General Information: In this verse Peter first instructs younger men specifically and then continues to instruct all of the believers.
Here, everyone refers to all the believers to whom Peter is writing this letter, and not to all people.
Peter speaks of humility as if it were a piece of clothing that a person could put on.
5:6: ὑπὸ τὴν κραταιὰν χεῖρα τοῦ Θεοῦ
Peter uses hand to refer to God’s power to save humble people and punish proud people.
Peter is using a spatial metaphor to describe God honoring someone as if God would lift that person up.
5:7: πᾶσαν τὴν μέριμναν ὑμῶν ἐπιρίψαντες ἐπ’ αὐτόν
Here Peter speaks of anxiety as if it were a heavy burden that a person can take off of his back and cast onto God.
5:8: The words translated as sober and watchful mean basically the same thing. Peter uses them to emphasize that believers need to be alert since the devil wants to destroy them.
ὡς λέων ὠρυόμενος περιπατεῖ, ζητῶν τινα καταπιεῖν

Peter speaks of the devil as if he were a roaring lion who wants to devour people. Just as a hungry lion devours its prey, the devil is seeking to destroy the faith of believers. See the discussion of this in the introduction for this chapter.
5:10: Here, in Christ refers to being united with Christ through faith in him.
Here, confirm, strengthen, and establish all mean basically the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize that God will fully strengthen people who suffer because they trust in Jesus.
5:12: Through Silvanus means that Silvanus wrote down the words that Peter told him to write in this letter. In ancient times it was common for people to use scribes to write down letters for them.
ταύτην εἶναι ἀληθῆ χάριν τοῦ Θεοῦ
Here the word grace refers to the gospel message, which tells of the kind things that God has done for believers.
Peter uses Stand to refer to being strongly committed to something as if someone is standing firmly in one place and refusing to move.
5:13: She and fellow-elect one here both refer to the group of believers who were with Peter when he wrote this letter.
See the discussion of this in the introduction to this chapter.
As was customary in this culture, Peter concludes the letter by extending greetings from people who are with him and who know the people to whom he is writing.
Peter refers to Mark as if he were his son, because he taught him about Christianity and loved him like a son.
5:14: A kiss was an action that expressed Christian affection in this culture. It showed the unity of those who belong to Christ.
εἰρήνη ὑμῖν πᾶσιν, τοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ
As was customary in his culture, Peter closes his letter with a blessing for his readers.
